- If sentiment shows strong bullish (≥0.5) or bearish (≤-1) momentum in recent days, model should adjust forecast directionally — avoid flat trends when sentiment is volatile.
- When model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows sharp drop or reversal, reduce forecast slope — especially after recent spikes.
- If true outcome is significantly higher than model (e.g., >5% above) and sentiment is neutral or bullish, model may be underestimating upward momentum — increase forecast slightly.
- If true outcome is significantly lower than model (e.g., >5% below) and sentiment is bearish, model may be overestimating — reduce forecast or add downward bias.
- Model tends to over-forecast in early periods after price spikes (e.g., 2024-04-30/05-01) — apply lag correction: reduce forecast by 1–2% for each day after a spike.
- Mean reversion is common in 30-day horizon — if model is trending sharply upward, consider smoothing or reducing slope after 3–5 consecutive days of high forecast.
- Sentiment history with multiple 0.00 entries suggests model should not ignore recent price action — if sentiment is flat, forecast should reflect recent volatility, not trend continuation.
- Overshoot after spikes (e.g., 2024-04-30) — model forecast peaks too early — reduce forecast by 2–5% for 3–5 days after spike.
- If sentiment turns negative after a spike, model should not continue upward — adjust forecast downward by 1–3% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
